Drug Patents: Money or Your Life

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Essential Cancer medications completely unaffordable for patients in South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
Many Cancer medications are pricey, with dying patients literally bankrupting themselves to try and stay alive. One good example is Lenalidomide, which is sold under the trade name, Revlimid. This medication is listed as an essential cancer medication by the WHO and is used for patients with Multiple Myeloma (Blood & Bone Marrow cancer) and a variety of other blood cancers. There is no cure for Multiple Myeloma and it's considered a long-term cronic disease. Patients need regular medication to prevent the progression of the disease - often for many years. Lenalidomide t/a Revlimid is priced at over R800,000 for year's supply in South Africa, and very few can afford it. Medical Aids pay up to about 80% (if you're lucky), depending on your medical aid... but co-payments are generally huge and many patients are struggling to afford it. Bear in mind that the patient faces additional expenses, and treatments and co-payments. If you don't have medical aid, you simply have no access to Lenalidomide. The State cannot afford to supply patients with this drug.

Summary:
Lenalidomide in the form of Revlimid, is patented by Celgene (USA). They also hold 32 patents for generics. In countries like India and Iran, it is not possible for one company to hold all the patents of a drug's generics, so there, competitors can manufacture alternatives, often at a fraction of the cost. In SA no-one can manufacture generics and importing generics have been very restricted. Up until 2016, SA patients could apply to import a generic of Lenalidomide from India at around 4% of the cost of the original. At the time the generic cost about R27,000 per year, compared to the R730,000 of the original, Revlimid. This import was done via Section 21 authorisations from the Medicine Control Council for importations. But noticing the loophole, Celgene, with the assistance of a South African pharmaceutical company (Key Oncologics (Pty) Ltd) stepped in and registered Lenalidomide with SAHPRA, The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. This meant that importing a generic became illegal. So at the moment Lenalidomide can only be bought in SA through Key Oncologics.

On top of that, South Africa’s patent system is geared towards monopoly holders and is at odds with the government’s constitutional obligation to take reasonable legislative steps to protect and promote the right to health of people living in South Africa. A revision in South Africa’s intellectual property policy could see the prices of medicines drop by as much as 90%, say Cancer Alliance and other NGO's fighting for the change in SA legislation. In SA, granting a patent is a simple administrative process. You pay a fee, tick the boxes and complete the paperwork. Big companies are taking advantage of this and acquiring patents for medicines, which blocks competition, thus creating situations where they can charge what they like, and patients have no option but to pay... or die.

Further information:
Lenalidomide is a derivative of thalidomide. Secondary patents could block access until 2026 – this is 71 years since the initial patent on thalidomide was granted in the US and 30 years after the initial lenalidomide patent was granted. These products are not available to the public sector patients mainly due to cost. Last year Celgene sold their patents to the company Bristol-Myers Squibb for US$74 BILLION.

A study conducted by Cancer Alliance shows that many of Celgene's patents that were rewarded in SA, were rejected in other regions of the world. In South Africa there is no appeals process or way to oppose the registration of a patent.

It is estimated that more than 80% of SA's Multiple Myeloma patients are in the public sector, which means the bulk of patients have no access to this important drug at all.

A CLEVER THOUGHT
Celgene held the exclusive patent to Thalidomide for 30 odd years. Then they "allowed" generics to enter the market, the price dropped ... to such an extent that this costs around R1500p/m now, affordably tot he State and public healthcare. But they also realised that people were becoming resistant to Thalidomide, and since Multiple Myeloma is a long-term illness, they realised that ALL patents would eventually have to move on to another drug. Lenalidomide. In the early 2000's Celgene patented Lenalidomide and over 75 generics world-wide... including 32 in South Africa. Pomalidomide is generation 3 in Celgene's range and is relatively new, but there are cases of some patients becoming resistant to Lenalidomide, who need to switch to Pomalidomide. Now all of a sudden, out of the blue (and thanks to mounting international pressure) Celgene (and Key Oncologics SA) are "allowing" a handful of generics on the market. The first is to be launched by Cipla in December. Although they will be cheaper, it will still not be affordable for the state, who cannot spend more than R5,000 per patient per month. But nevertheless... they hold the exclusive patent on Pomalidomide... the next drug in line which sells for R94,000 per month's supply. So, a clever PR exercise... because they know that Multiple Myeloma patients live for many years and need meds for many years and WILL eventually become resistant to Lenalidmide and will need the new meds.

ADDITIONAL CASE STUDY INFO
Jayne Hewison is fabulous. She was diagnosed with Multiple Myeloma ten years ago. She was originally on Thalidomide, became resistant and had to move to Lenalidomide. She basically bankrupted herself trying to afford the meds. Lost her house, sold all her jewelry and other stuff. Then she started importing it illegally. And she's happy to say that on camera. She grew resistant to the Lenalidomide and started using another drug -- equally expensive. Now, because of complications she has had to move onto Pomalidomide (the 3rd installment in Celgene/Key Oncologics's empire. Officially, the meds cost R94,000 per month!
Teboho Shai unfortunately passed away a little while ago, but I'm trying to organise to speak to a family member about his struggle with meds.

EXPERTS
Will speak to someone from CIPLA, Cancer Alliance and hopefully SAHPRA

Script:


Drug Patents -- MASTER


Baba Shai
Teboho was a good husband. He was self-driven and ambitious.
V/O
Teboho Shai passed away in March this year after a 4-year long battle with Cancer. Shortly after being diagnosed in 2016, Shai became wheelchair bound and his wife Baba, resigned from her job to take care of her husband...
Baba Shai
Because of financial constraints we were forced to relocate so that we could be closer to our family.
V/O
The income from Shai’s business was simply not enough to cover the family’s expenses.
Baba Shai
We were on medical aid. It costed us something like R70,000 for a month and the medical aid would only pay 20% of that which was unaffordable for us.
LINK
Being diagnosed with Cancer is a shock for anybody but imagine finding out that the medication you need to keep the disease under control is totally unaffordable.
V/O
Shai’s situation is not unique. Many cancer patients in South Africa struggle to cover the steep costs of the medication they need...which is often exacerbated by our outdated patent legislation’s shortcomings, says Tendai Mafuma, a legal researcher at the NGO, SECTION27.
Tendai Mafuma
If you’re a pharmaceutical company and you developed a medicine, you are able to patent it for 20 years in South Africa.
V/O
Once registered, Act No. 57 of 1978 entitles the patent-holder exclusive rights to manufacture, import, market and sell their product.
Tendai Mafuma
When you have one person who is able to make the medicine, and they’re able to peg the price for that medicine wherever because there is no competition uh you get into a situation where some medicine for example cancer medicines are very expensive.
V/O
The cancer that claimed Shai’s life is a blood cancer called Multiple Myeloma. Haematologist, Dr Karen Gunther has been treating myeloma patients for many years.
Karen Gunther
It's a tumor essentially of the immune system of the plasma cells and has all these different effects on all the different organ systems.
SALOMÉ Meyer
It is a disease that they ultimately will live with for the rest of their lives.
V/O
Salome Meyer from Cancer Alliance advocates for accessible cancer treatments for patients, including those living with Multiple Myeloma.
Salome Meyer
Depending on the availability of as well, then obviously as the affordability of medicines, you can extend the patient's life with quite a number of years.
V/O
In addition to other therapies like chemo and steroids, patients with Multiple Myeloma benefit hugely from immunomodulatory drugs referred to as IMiDs.
Karen Gunther
IMiDs have been absolute key drugs in treating myeloma, particularly in modifying the immune system to maintain remissions. And they really have been game changers in the field.
V/O
The original drug in this chain of special immunomodulatory medicines is called Thalidomide - a drug that made headlines 70 years ago.
LINK
Thalidomide was originally developed in the 1950’s as a sedative or tranquilizer and quickly became known as a miracle drug and widely prescribed to pregnant women for nausea. But it turned out to be one of the biggest man-made medical disasters in modern history.
V/O
But in just a few years over 40 countries reported thousands of miscarriages and babies born with severe deformities, linked to Thalidomide use. The drug was taken off the market, but ongoing research on Thalidomide revealed the drug’s unique properties to treat various blood cancers, particularly Multiple Myeloma. By the late 90’s it was reintroduced to the market and is still widely used.
Dr Karen Gunter
The problem with the Thalidomide is the damage to the nerves in starting at the ends of the nerves and the fingers and toes. The longer you use it the more likely you are to develop irreversible side-effects.
V/O
Fortunately an enhanced, second-generation drug was derived from Thalidomide around the turn of the century. With far fewer side-effects, and greater efficacy, Lenalidomide was set to change the lives of people living with Multiple Myeloma.
Karen Gunther
Lenalidomide is standard of care internationally -- first line therapy and maintenance therapy for all patients with myeloma. So it's considered a key drug in the management of myeloma.
V/O
In 2019 it was added to the WHO’s list of essential medications, but at the cost of Lenalidomide in South Africa very few have access. In fact, if you rely on public healthcare you will only have access to the original drug, Thalidomide.
Dr Karen Gunther
I worked in state for a long time, and that was one of the reasons I left. I couldn't bear the fact that there's stuff out there that will help people and you just can't do anything.
V/O
Lenalidomide -- branded as Revlimid -- is patented in South Africa by Key Oncologics (Pty) Ltd. Over the past decade the price of the drug has fluctuated between about R75,000 and R40,000 for a month’s treatment.
Karen Gunther
The sad story about myeloma, is that you live as long as you can afford to live.
Jayne Hewison
We had sold our house in KZN and that money all disappeared into Lenalidomide. Anything we had of value we sold.
V/O
Jayne Hewison has been on a decade-long journey with Multiple Myeloma.
Jayne Hewison
My haematologist said there's nothing more we can do for you because you can't afford the medication. So you're going to have to think about are you going to go to hospice or what are we going to do here?
Dr Karen Gunther
Claire: Do some people fall off treatment just because they can't afford the medication?
Dr: Yeah, for sure. For sure. And we stop treatments too soon and we don't choose the optimal treatments.
V/O
Acquiring any patent is a fairly simple administrative process in this country, says Mafuma.
Tendai Mafuma
You just file some papers and if you say that your patent meets the criteria it’s granted to you. They don’t actually go to the invention, inspect it to make sure that it meets the things that you are saying.
V/O
So without anyone actually checking the efficacy or the novelty of your product you get instant protection from competition… and we also don’t have systems in place that allow civil society to question or oppose patents…
Tendai Mafuma
In other countries they have systems called patent oppositions, which means that when someone files their papers with the authorities to get a patent, civil society organisations or anyone interested has access to those papers. And they can look at them and actually oppose the granting of that patent.
V/O
In addition to the patent of Revlimid itself, Key Oncologics has registered an additional 32 secondary patents related to lenalidomide, which could shield them from generic competition up until 2028. And what is more, their patented 3rd generation IMiD, called Pomalidomide, was registered for the South African market earlier this year.
Salome Meyer
They came in with a price of eighty five thousand rand a month. It makes your eyes water if you think that the patient has to pay eighty five thousand rand just for one medicine.
LINK
While the debate around whether or not it is ethical to sell life-saving medication at 40, 60 or even 80 thousand rand rages, it’s important to remember that Key Oncologics hasn’t broken any laws in South Africa.
V/O
In a written response, Key Oncologics states that they are a representative of Celgene, a Bristol Myers Squibb company that dictates the pricing which is based on the value they deliver. They say they support policies that reduce unnecessary regulations, promote competition, and the development process.

But in spite of this, for many Myeloma patients there is only one answer...
Jayne Hewison
If you want to stay alive you’re going to make a plan. So, at the age of 63 I’ve become a criminal druggy…
V/O
Many patients end up illegally importing their Lenalidomide from countries like India, where patent laws are more progressive, where it is not so easy to get blanket protection for your product, and where competition flourishes.
Jayne Hewison
I was getting it for two thousand five hundred rand a month compared to, at that point, forty four thousand rand a month.
V/O
Meanwhile, local pharmaceutical companies are looking to challenge Key Oncologics’ dominance over the South African market.
Salome Meyer
Now there are five companies that were able to register the generic form of Lenalidomide in South Africa.
V/O
Eurolab’s CEO Lynne du Toit, is adamant that their Lenalidomide brand will become a market player.
Lynne du Toit
We are absolutely determined to fight this patent. We cannot stand by when we have a registered product at a hugely affordable price and watch these patients suffer.
V/O
While it is still uncertain if this legal battle can and will be won, there is an air of optimism in the Myeloma community.
Salome Meyer
Into the first quarter of twenty twenty one, we are going to see a price war in South Africa with regards to Lenalidomide.


Baba Shai
Claire: How would he feel about this?
He would be very very happy. We have been fighting for the generic to be released in South Africa for many years. It would be too late for him now but if it does happen, it would benefit those who have been fighting with this cancer.


* * *







PROMO 1
We investigate how outdated legislation is costing Cancer patients dearly, even forcing them to break the law. What can be done to get much-needed drugs to those who suffer?




PROMO 2
A cancer pill that costs less than R3000 in India, sells for over R40,000 per month in South Africa. How are our outdated patent laws limiting patients’ access to medication?




PROMO 3
When diagnosed with terminal cancer, access to effective medication is a situation of life or death... but what happens if, even with medical aid, you simply cannot afford it.

Tendai Mafuma When you have one person who is able to make the medicine, and they’re able to peg the price for that medicine wherever because there is no competition uh you get into a situation where some medicine for example cancer medicines are very expensive. V/O The cancer that claimed Shai’s life is a blood cancer called Multiple Myeloma. Haematologist, Dr Karen Gunther has been treating myeloma patients for many years. Karen Gunther It's a tumor essentially of the immune system of the plasma cells and has all these different effects on all the different organ systems. SALOMÉ Meyer It is a disease that they ultimately will live with for the rest of their lives. V/O Salome Meyer from Cancer Alliance advocates for accessible cancer treatments for patients, including those living with Multiple Myeloma. Salome Meyer Depending on the availability of as well, then obviously as the affordability of medicines, you can extend the patient's life with quite a number of years. V/O In addition to other therapies like chemo and steroids, patients with Multiple Myeloma benefit hugely from immunomodulatory drugs referred to as IMiDs. Karen Gunther IMiDs have been absolute key drugs in treating myeloma, particularly in modifying the immune system to maintain remissions. And they really have been game changers in the field. V/O The original drug in this chain of special immunomodulatory medicines is called Thalidomide - a drug that made headlines 70 years ago. LINK Thalidomide was originally developed in the 1950’s as a sedative or tranquilizer and quickly became known as a miracle drug and widely prescribed to pregnant women for nausea. But it turned out to be one of the biggest man-made medical disasters in modern history. V/O But in just a few years over 40 countries reported thousands of miscarriages and babies born with severe deformities, linked to Thalidomide use. The drug was taken off the market, but ongoing research on Thalidomide revealed the drug’s unique properties to treat various blood cancers, particularly Multiple Myeloma. By the late 90’s it was reintroduced to the market and is still widely used. Dr Karen Gunter The problem with the Thalidomide is the damage to the nerves in starting at the ends of the nerves and the fingers and toes. The longer you use it the more likely you are to develop irreversible side-effects. V/O Fortunately an enhanced, second-generation drug was derived from Thalidomide around the turn of the century. With far fewer side-effects, and greater efficacy, Lenalidomide was set to change the lives of people living with Multiple Myeloma. Karen Gunther Lenalidomide is standard of care internationally -- first line therapy and maintenance therapy for all patients with myeloma. So it's considered a key drug in the management of myeloma. V/O In 2019 it was added to the WHO’s list of essential medications, but at the cost of Lenalidomide in South Africa very few have access. In fact, if you rely on public healthcare you will only have access to the original drug, Thalidomide. Dr Karen Gunther I worked in state for a long time, and that was one of the reasons I left. I couldn't bear the fact that there's stuff out there that will help people and you just can't do anything. V/O Lenalidomide -- branded as Revlimid -- is patented in South Africa by Key Oncologics (Pty) Ltd. Over the past decade the price of the drug has fluctuated between about R75,000 and R40,000 for a month’s treatment. Karen Gunther The sad story about myeloma, is that you live as long as you can afford to live. Jayne Hewison We had sold our house in KZN and that money all disappeared into Lenalidomide. Anything we had of value we sold. V/O Jayne Hewison has been on a decade-long journey with Multiple Myeloma. Jayne Hewison My haematologist said there's nothing more we can do for you because you can't afford the medication. So you're going to have to think about are you going to go to hospice or what are we going to do here? Dr Karen Gunther Claire: Do some people fall off treatment just because they can't afford the medication? Dr: Yeah, for sure. For sure. And we stop treatments too soon and we don't choose the optimal treatments. V/O Acquiring any patent is a fairly simple administrative process in this country, says Mafuma. Tendai Mafuma You just file some papers and if you say that your patent meets the criteria it’s granted to you. They don’t actually go to the invention, inspect it to make sure that it meets the things that you are saying. V/O So without anyone actually checking the efficacy or the novelty of your product you get instant protection from competition… and we also don’t have systems in place that allow civil society to question or oppose patents… Tendai Mafuma In other countries they have systems called patent oppositions, which means that when someone files their papers with the authorities to get a patent, civil society organisations or anyone interested has access to those papers. And they can look at them and actually oppose the granting of that patent. V/O In addition to the patent of Revlimid itself, Key Oncologics has registered an additional 32 secondary patents related to lenalidomide, which could shield them from generic competition up until 2028. And what is more, their patented 3rd generation IMiD, called Pomalidomide, was registered for the South African market earlier this year. Salome Meyer They came in with a price of eighty five thousand rand a month. It makes your eyes water if you think that the patient has to pay eighty five thousand rand just for one medicine. LINK While the debate around whether or not it is ethical to sell life-saving medication at 40, 60 or even 80 thousand rand rages, it’s important to remember that Key Oncologics hasn’t broken any laws in South Africa. V/O In a written response, Key Oncologics states that they are a representative of Celgene, a Bristol Myers Squibb company that dictates the pricing which is based on the value they deliver. They say they support policies that reduce unnecessary regulations, promote competition, and the development process. But in spite of this, for many Myeloma patients there is only one answer... Jayne Hewison If you want to stay alive you’re going to make a plan. So, at the age of 63 I’ve become a criminal druggy… V/O Many patients end up illegally importing their Lenalidomide from countries like India, where patent laws are more progressive, where it is not so easy to get blanket protection for your product, and where competition flourishes. Jayne Hewison I was getting it for two thousand five hundred rand a month compared to, at that point, forty four thousand rand a month. V/O Meanwhile, local pharmaceutical companies are looking to challenge Key Oncologics’ dominance over the South African market. Salome Meyer Now there are five companies that were able to register the generic form of Lenalidomide in South Africa. V/O Eurolab’s CEO Lynne du Toit, is adamant that their Lenalidomide brand will become a market player. Lynne du Toit We are absolutely determined to fight this patent. We cannot stand by when we have a registered product at a hugely affordable price and watch these patients suffer. V/O While it is still uncertain if this legal battle can and will be won, there is an air of optimism in the Myeloma community. Salome Meyer Into the first quarter of twenty twenty one, we are going to see a price war in South Africa with regards to Lenalidomide. Baba Shai Claire: How would he feel about this? He would be very very happy. We have been fighting for the generic to be released in South Africa for many years. It would be too late for him now but if it does happen, it would benefit those who have been fighting with this cancer. * * * PROMO 1 We investigate how outdated legislation is costing Cancer patients dearly, even forcing them to break the law. What can be done to get much-needed drugs to those who suffer? PROMO 2 A cancer pill that costs less than R3000 in India, sells for over R40,000 per month in South Africa. How are our outdated patent laws limiting patients’ access to medication? PROMO 3 When diagnosed with terminal cancer, access to effective medication is a situation of life or death... but what happens if, even with medical aid, you simply cannot afford it.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Essential Cancer medications completely unaffordable for patients in South Africa.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Many Cancer medications are pricey, with dying patients literally bankrupting themselves to try and stay alive. One good example is Lenalidomide, which is sold under the trade name, Revlimid. This medication is listed as an essential cancer medication by the WHO and is used for patients with Multiple Myeloma (Blood & Bone Marrow cancer) and a variety of other blood cancers. There is no cure for Multiple Myeloma and it's considered a long-term cronic disease. Patients need regular medication to prevent the progression of the disease - often for many years. Lenalidomide t/a Revlimid is priced at over R800,000 for year's supply in South Africa, and very few can afford it. Medical Aids pay up to about 80% (if you're lucky), depending on your medical aid... but co-payments are generally huge and many patients are struggling to afford it. Bear in mind that the patient faces additional expenses, and treatments and co-payments. If you don't have medical aid, you simply have no access to Lenalidomide. The State cannot afford to supply patients with this drug.
metadata.Summary: Lenalidomide in the form of Revlimid, is patented by Celgene (USA). They also hold 32 patents for generics. In countries like India and Iran, it is not possible for one company to hold all the patents of a drug's generics, so there, competitors can manufacture alternatives, often at a fraction of the cost. In SA no-one can manufacture generics and importing generics have been very restricted. Up until 2016, SA patients could apply to import a generic of Lenalidomide from India at around 4% of the cost of the original. At the time the generic cost about R27,000 per year, compared to the R730,000 of the original, Revlimid. This import was done via Section 21 authorisations from the Medicine Control Council for importations. But noticing the loophole, Celgene, with the assistance of a South African pharmaceutical company (Key Oncologics (Pty) Ltd) stepped in and registered Lenalidomide with SAHPRA, The South African Health Products Regulatory Authority. This meant that importing a generic became illegal. So at the moment Lenalidomide can only be bought in SA through Key Oncologics. On top of that, South Africa’s patent system is geared towards monopoly holders and is at odds with the government’s constitutional obligation to take reasonable legislative steps to protect and promote the right to health of people living in South Africa. A revision in South Africa’s intellectual property policy could see the prices of medicines drop by as much as 90%, say Cancer Alliance and other NGO's fighting for the change in SA legislation. In SA, granting a patent is a simple administrative process. You pay a fee, tick the boxes and complete the paperwork. Big companies are taking advantage of this and acquiring patents for medicines, which blocks competition, thus creating situations where they can charge what they like, and patients have no option but to pay... or die.
metadata.Further information: Lenalidomide is a derivative of thalidomide. Secondary patents could block access until 2026 – this is 71 years since the initial patent on thalidomide was granted in the US and 30 years after the initial lenalidomide patent was granted. These products are not available to the public sector patients mainly due to cost. Last year Celgene sold their patents to the company Bristol-Myers Squibb for US$74 BILLION. A study conducted by Cancer Alliance shows that many of Celgene's patents that were rewarded in SA, were rejected in other regions of the world. In South Africa there is no appeals process or way to oppose the registration of a patent. It is estimated that more than 80% of SA's Multiple Myeloma patients are in the public sector, which means the bulk of patients have no access to this important drug at all. A CLEVER THOUGHT Celgene held the exclusive patent to Thalidomide for 30 odd years. Then they "allowed" generics to enter the market, the price dropped ... to such an extent that this costs around R1500p/m now, affordably tot he State and public healthcare. But they also realised that people were becoming resistant to Thalidomide, and since Multiple Myeloma is a long-term illness, they realised that ALL patents would eventually have to move on to another drug. Lenalidomide. In the early 2000's Celgene patented Lenalidomide and over 75 generics world-wide... including 32 in South Africa. Pomalidomide is generation 3 in Celgene's range and is relatively new, but there are cases of some patients becoming resistant to Lenalidomide, who need to switch to Pomalidomide. Now all of a sudden, out of the blue (and thanks to mounting international pressure) Celgene (and Key Oncologics SA) are "allowing" a handful of generics on the market. The first is to be launched by Cipla in December. Although they will be cheaper, it will still not be affordable for the state, who cannot spend more than R5,000 per patient per month. But nevertheless... they hold the exclusive patent on Pomalidomide... the next drug in line which sells for R94,000 per month's supply. So, a clever PR exercise... because they know that Multiple Myeloma patients live for many years and need meds for many years and WILL eventually become resistant to Lenalidmide and will need the new meds. ADDITIONAL CASE STUDY INFO Jayne Hewison is fabulous. She was diagnosed with Multiple Myeloma ten years ago. She was originally on Thalidomide, became resistant and had to move to Lenalidomide. She basically bankrupted herself trying to afford the meds. Lost her house, sold all her jewelry and other stuff. Then she started importing it illegally. And she's happy to say that on camera. She grew resistant to the Lenalidomide and started using another drug -- equally expensive. Now, because of complications she has had to move onto Pomalidomide (the 3rd installment in Celgene/Key Oncologics's empire. Officially, the meds cost R94,000 per month! Teboho Shai unfortunately passed away a little while ago, but I'm trying to organise to speak to a family member about his struggle with meds. EXPERTS Will speak to someone from CIPLA, Cancer Alliance and hopefully SAHPRA
